spec: trustless-ai/deils "leg 2" (Merlini's held-content-behind-commitment design), pinned in Telegram msg_id 1623 (case ownership), 1632/2111-2112 (canonicalization + ref-string format correction). Reference implementation: invinoveritas POST /prove {disclose:false} + POST /prove/{proof_id}/reveal.
ref_format: "sha256:" + 64 lowercase hex. NOT "0x"+hex -- corrected msg_id 2111/2112, matches invinoveritas's own decision_ref convention.
canonicalization: RFC 8785 JCS: recursively sorted object keys, compact separators (no whitespace), raw UTF-8 (not \uXXXX-escaped). Equivalent to Python json.dumps(v, sort_keys=True, separators=(',',':'), ensure_ascii=False).
commitment_hash_definition: "sha256:" + sha256(jcs(parsed(content))).hexdigest() -- the input to jcs() is ALWAYS the parsed (language-native dict/object) form of the content, never whatever wire encoding it happened to arrive in. Pinned explicitly (Pavlo, trustless-ai group, 2026-07-31) after the escaped_non_ascii_wire_trap vector below showed the failure mode: hashing a served \uXXXX-escaped JSON string (even though it is byte-for-byte valid, parseable JSON) is WRONG, because that string is not the canonical form -- only re-canonicalizing the PARSED value is. Putting `parsed()` in the rule itself (not just in a test vector) closes the domain ambiguity at the definition, not just at the checker.

cases.description: Happy path: revealed content hashes to the published commitment exactly.
Same content, different input key order -- MUST still bind. Proves the shared canonical JSON does the work, not string-equality.
One byte of revealed content changed (artifact_hash's last char) -- MUST be content_commitment_mismatch. Proves the check says NO loudly, no silent pass.
Nothing disclosed yet -- pending, not a failure. No revealed_content is submitted; the checker must not attempt a recompute over unbound content.

Deliberately-wrong-obvious-answer case (Correctover-style, distinct from the top-level near-miss above): keys are shuffled at MULTIPLE NESTED LEVELS, not just the top level. A checker that only sorts top-level keys, or does a raw string diff instead of a recursive JCS canonicalization, would report this as a mismatch (or falsely pass without ever canonicalizing). The correct recursive canonicalization must still bind.

Byte-domain ambiguity (Pavlo, trustless-ai group, 2026-07-31, extending Merlini's own escaping-catch note from the PQ-key-binding close): the commitment is over raw UTF-8 JCS bytes (ensure_ascii=False), but a relay/consumer that re-serializes the revealed content with a DEFAULT json.dumps (ensure_ascii=True, \uXXXX-escaped non-ASCII) produces DIFFERENT bytes for the same logical content. A checker that hashes the served WIRE STRING directly (byte-level, no re-parse) gets the WRONG digest and would report a false content_commitment_mismatch on genuinely identical content. The correct check always parses THEN re-canonicalizes (JCS, ensure_ascii=False) before hashing -- it must never trust or hash the wire bytes as-received. `wire_representation_ascii_escaped` is what a relay doing plain json.dumps(content) (ensure_ascii's stdlib default) would actually serve; `wire_byte_hash_must_not_match_commitment` pins that hashing those bytes directly is WRONG, not just undocumented risk.
